items.title: Steve Turré interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 29, 2021
items.q: I played with Dizzy, McCoy Tyner, Woody Shaw, Cedar, all the — we never, we never talk about modes

ctx.x: The fact that you played a melodic instrument plus you played the bass, I would think that that gave you an added perspective on how music worked, and you’re hearing the, providing the bass notes and hearing the chords on top of it. I’m not sure there’s a question here except that I think the bass is so important to all the music we play and improvisation also — being able to hear the low end.

Well you know in New Orleans traditional music the trombone is like a quasi-bass at times. And you know you touch on the bass and then you go up and do some other stuff, but it’s connected. And of course you know you don’t have a chord without a root, you know, but then you know as my ears have developed you can take a chord and move the root around. And the colors change but it’s still the same chord. You know I’ll tell you something I played with Dizzy, McCoy Tyner, Woody Shaw, Cedar, all the — we never, we…

B flat scale but you’re starting on an E or E flat or whatever. It’s just, that’s the color. That’s the tonality. By moving the root you change the color. But you know, for instance, I was asking McCoy Tyner what he played on the — mostly they call it the altered chord. Altered how? What does altered mean? It’s the raise 5, raise 9. That’s what they mean. Plus 5, plus 9. You know a lot of McCoy’s music has that in there. And you know I could approximate the sound but there was something I was missing. And I asked…

items.title: Tyner McCoy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] So you had Virgil Jones, Steve Turre, Frank Lacy, John Clark, so again, truly a big band... [INTERVIEWEE] The older guys.

ctx.x: No, first it was Steve Davis, then Jimmy.
So Steve and then Jimmy, but you played with Billy Higgins?
Yeah he played with Billy, traveled with Billy too.
